title: Acute arsenic poisoning: give dimercaprol
vignette: A 17-year-old girl with a history of depression is brought to the emergency department after a suicide attempt. Her parents report that she ingested 2 bottles of insecticide following an argument with her sister approximately 2 hours prior to presentation. The patient's symptoms include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and copious watery diarrhea. She has a known history of self-cutting and suicidal ideation but no prior suicide attempts. Blood pressure is 86/42 mm Hg and pulse is 120/min. Her breath has a faint garlic odor, and she has numerous healing linear scars on her forearms. Which of the following medications should be administered immediately?

clues.note: Insecticides/pesticides are a classic source of arsenic. An intentional ingestion of a large volume points to acute heavy-metal poisoning.
Acute arsenic poisoning causes profuse vomiting and watery ('rice-water') diarrhea from GI mucosal injury, leading to large fluid losses.
Hypotension (86/42 / normal ~120/80 mm Hg) with tachycardia reflects hypovolemic shock from massive GI fluid loss - and arsenic can also cause cardiovascular collapse and QT prolongation.
A garlic odor on the breath is the classic tell of acute arsenic poisoning, distinguishing it from the other listed toxins.

whatMatters: Insecticide ingestion + severe GI symptoms (vomiting, watery diarrhea) + hypotension + GARLIC breath odor = acute arsenic poisoning. The first-line chelator is DIMERCAPROL (British anti-Lewisite), which supplies sulfhydryl groups that bind arsenic and displace it from enzymes. Answer C. Also give IV fluids; oral succimer (DMSA) is used for milder/less-acute cases.
strategy: Pattern-match the toxidrome to the metal, then the metal to its chelator. Garlic breath + watery diarrhea + insecticide = arsenic -> dimercaprol (or DMSA). Then map the other chelators to their toxins: CaNa2EDTA/succimer = lead; deferoxamine/deferasirox = iron; hydroxocobalamin/nitrites/thiosulfate = cyanide; methylene blue = methemoglobinemia.

eliminations.label: CaNa2EDTA - lead chelator
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: calcium disodium EDTA chelates LEAD (poisoning causes constipation, anemia with basophilic stippling, neuropathy). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: wrong metal - the garlic breath and watery diarrhea point to arsenic. ✅ Correct if: lead poisoning.

eliminations.label: Deferoxamine - iron chelator
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: deferoxamine binds IRON in acute iron overdose/overload (vomiting, GI bleeding, metabolic acidosis). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: this is arsenic, not iron. ✅ Correct if: acute iron ingestion (e.g., prenatal vitamins) or transfusional overload.

eliminations.label: Hydroxycobalamin - cyanide antidote
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: hydroxocobalamin (a B12 precursor) binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin (excreted in urine). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: cyanide causes flushing/'cherry-red' skin and lactic acidosis - not garlic breath from insecticide. ✅ Correct if: cyanide poisoning.

eliminations.label: Methylene blue - methemoglobinemia, your pick
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: methylene blue reduces methemoglobin (via NADPH) in methemoglobinemia (cyanosis unresponsive to O2, 'chocolate-colored' blood). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: this patient has arsenic poisoning, not methemoglobinemia. The trap is picking an ED antidote, but methylene blue treats a different toxin. ✅ Correct if: methemoglobinemia (e.g., from dapsone, nitrites, benzocaine).

reasoning: Insecticide ingestion + vomiting/watery diarrhea + hypotension + garlic breath = acute arsenic poisoning
Arsenic binds sulfhydryl groups and disrupts cellular respiration
Dimercaprol donates thiol groups that chelate arsenic and displace it from enzymes
mechanism: Arsenic (found in pesticides/insecticides, contaminated water, and pressure-treated wood) binds sulfhydryl (thiol) groups, inhibiting sulfhydryl-containing enzymes - notably pyruvate dehydrogenase - and disrupting cellular respiration and gluconeogenesis. Acute poisoning causes profuse vomiting and watery ('rice-water') diarrhea with hypovolemic hypotension, a garlic odor on the breath, and QT prolongation that can progress to torsades de pointes. First-line chelation is dimercaprol (British anti-Lewisite), whose vicinal thiol groups bind arsenic and displace it from enzyme sulfhydryls, increasing urinary excretion; oral succimer (DMSA) is used for milder cases, along with supportive IV fluids. The distractor antidotes target different toxins (EDTA/succimer for lead, deferoxamine for iron, hydroxocobalamin for cyanide, methylene blue for methemoglobinemia).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocabulary
difficulty.message: Unsure on chelator, sulfhydryl/thiol, dimercaprol/BAL, succimer/DMSA, or methemoglobinemia? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🧲 Pulled by a distractor
difficulty.message: Each option is the antidote for a DIFFERENT toxin: EDTA (lead), deferoxamine (iron), hydroxocobalamin (cyanide), methylene blue (methemoglobinemia - your pick).

difficulty.label: ✍️ Something else
difficulty.message: Bank: garlic breath + rice-water diarrhea after insecticide = arsenic -> dimercaprol (BAL); oral succimer for milder cases.
